course.title: Php
course.description: A complete practical PHP course progressing from modern language foundations through object-oriented programming, HTTP applications, sessions, PDO, secure coding, Composer, testing, architecture, performance, deployment, and a final secure task API.
prerequisites: Basic programming logic is helpful but not mandatory
A local PHP development environment and text editor
learningOutcomes: Explain PHP execution in CLI and web environments.
Write typed maintainable PHP using functions, arrays, exceptions, and objects.
Build validated HTTP endpoints and JSON APIs.
Implement authentication state with sessions and password hashing.
Use PDO prepared statements and transactions with relational databases.
Apply output encoding, CSRF, upload, and secret-management controls.
Manage dependencies with Composer and write automated tests.
Reason about performance, deployment, and version maintenance.
Build and explain a realistic secure PHP application.

modules.title: Foundations and Execution
modules.description: Start with the PHP runtime, syntax, types, control flow, and functions.

lessons.title: Runtime, Versions, and First Script
lessons.description: Install a supported PHP runtime and understand CLI versus web execution.
learningObjectives: install or select a supported PHP release
run a PHP script from the CLI

notes.text: PHP is a general-purpose scripting language especially suited to web development. The official site currently lists PHP 8.5 as the current stable branch; PHP 8.6 beta is a testing release, not a production target.
Use php -v and php --ini to identify the CLI interpreter and its configuration.
The built-in development server is useful for local learning and testing; it is not a production deployment architecture.

summary: PHP can execute scripts from the command line and can also run as part of a web-server deployment.

lessons.title: Syntax, Variables, and Types
lessons.description: Build correct PHP expressions and understand the main PHP value types.

notes.text: Variables begin with $. PHP supports null, bool, int, float, string, arrays, objects and resources.
declare(strict_types=1) makes scalar type checking stricter for calls originating in that file; it does not turn every PHP operation into a statically typed operation.

summary: Types and explicit contracts make application behavior easier to reason about.

lessons.title: Operators and Control Flow
lessons.description: Use comparisons, branches, loops, and match expressions.

notes.text: = assigns. == performs a non-strict comparison that can involve type juggling. === compares both type and value.
match is an expression and its arms use identity comparison.

summary: Control flow expresses program decisions; choose the construct that makes the decision easiest to read.

lessons.title: Functions and Scope
lessons.description: Create reusable functions with clear input and output contracts.

notes.text:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);
function total(int ...$values): int {
    return array_sum($values);
}
echo total(10, 20, 30);

practicals.title: Build a typed score analyzer
practicals.description: Practice CLI input, validation, typed functions, and match.
steps: Return a grade with a typed function.
practicals.solution:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);
function grade(int $s): string {
    return match (true) {
        $s >= 90 => 'A',
        $s >= 80 => 'B',
        $s >= 70 => 'C',
        default => 'D',
    };
}
$score=(int)($argv[1]??0);
echo grade($score),PHP_EOL;
practicals.output: The program prints the calculated grade.

summary: Functions should have focused responsibilities and explicit contracts.

tasks.title: Typed score analyzer
tasks.problemStatement: Accept one score, validate 0–100, and print its grade.
requirements: PHP 8.5 or another supported PHP branch
tasks.solutionCode:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);
$raw=$argv[1]??'';
if(!is_numeric($raw)){fwrite(STDERR,"Score must be numeric
");exit(1);}
$score=(int)$raw;
if($score<0||$score>100){fwrite(STDERR,"Score must be 0-100
");exit(1);}
function grade(int $s):string{return match(true){$s>=90=>'A',$s>=80=>'B',$s>=70=>'C',default=>'D'};}
echo grade($score),PHP_EOL;
tasks.solutionExplanation: The boundary is validated before the pure grading function is called.

modules.title: Collections, Text, JSON, and Errors
modules.description: Transform arrays and strings, exchange JSON, handle files, and propagate failures.

lessons.title: Arrays and Iteration
lessons.description: Use indexed and associative arrays and iterate safely.

notes.text: PHP arrays are ordered maps and can be used as list-like or map-like structures.

$users=[['id'=>1,'email'=>'a@example.test'],['id'=>2,'email'=>'b@example.test']];
foreach($users as $user){ echo $user['email'],PHP_EOL; }

summary: Choose array operations based on the data shape and keep key assumptions explicit.

lessons.title: Strings and JSON
lessons.description: Manipulate text and safely encode/decode JSON.

notes.text: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR makes JSON failures visible as JsonException rather than requiring silent return-value checking.
Decoded request data is still untrusted input and must be validated.

summary: JSON is a serialization boundary, not an authorization mechanism.

lessons.title: Files and Exceptions
lessons.description: Work with filesystem APIs and structured error handling.

notes.text: Filesystem operations can fail because of paths, permissions, encoding, or missing files. Handle expected failure deliberately.
Production applications should log useful diagnostic details without returning stack traces or secrets to users.

summary: Exceptions allow lower-level code to report failure while higher-level code decides how to recover.

tasks.title: Safe JSON configuration reader
tasks.description: Read and validate a JSON configuration file.
tasks.problemStatement: Distinguish missing files, invalid JSON, and valid configuration data.
tasks.hint: Validate the decoded value before accessing keys.
tasks.solutionCode:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);
$path=$argv[1]??'config.json';
if(!is_file($path)){fwrite(STDERR,"File not found
");exit(1);}
try{
 $data=json_decode(file_get_contents($path),true,512,JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
 if(!is_array($data)) throw new RuntimeException('Configuration must be an object');
 foreach(['app_name','environment'] as $k) if(!array_key_exists($k,$data)) throw new RuntimeException("Missing $k");
 echo "Configuration valid
";
}catch(JsonException $e){fwrite(STDERR,"Invalid JSON
");exit(1);}
catch(RuntimeException $e){fwrite(STDERR,$e->getMessage()."
");exit(1);}
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution validates the filesystem boundary, JSON syntax, decoded shape, and required fields.

modules.title: Object-Oriented PHP
modules.description: Model application behavior with classes, interfaces, inheritance, traits, namespaces, and exceptions.

lessons.title: Classes, Properties, and Methods
lessons.description: Design classes with typed properties, constructors, and encapsulation.

notes.text: Typed properties must be initialized before access.

summary: Classes package state and behavior behind explicit contracts.

lessons.title: Interfaces, Inheritance, and Traits
lessons.description: Use interfaces for contracts and inheritance or traits only where they fit the design.

notes.text: Interfaces allow callers to depend on behavior rather than a specific implementation.
Composition is often preferable to inheritance when behavior can be assembled from collaborators.

summary: Interfaces are useful dependency boundaries, especially for testing.

lessons.title: Namespaces, Exceptions, and Autoloading
lessons.description: Organize larger applications with namespaces and Composer autoloading.

notes.text: Composer can generate an autoloader from project configuration, reducing manual require statements.

summary: Namespaces prevent naming collisions and Composer makes class loading predictable.

tasks.title: Interface-based notification service
tasks.description: Create a notification service that depends on an interface.
tasks.problemStatement: Implement a NotificationSender interface and a log sender; inject it into a service.
tasks.objectives: Use interfaces and constructor dependency injection.
tasks.hint: Program to the interface, not the concrete sender.
tasks.solutionCode:
<?php
interface NotificationSender { public function send(string $to,string $message):void; }
final class LogSender implements NotificationSender {
 public function send(string $to,string $message):void { error_log("To $to: $message"); }
}
final class NotificationService {
 public function __construct(private NotificationSender $sender){}
 public function notify(string $to,string $message):void{$this->sender->send($to,$message);}
}
$service=new NotificationService(new LogSender());
$service->notify('user@example.test','Welcome');
tasks.solutionExplanation: The service can be tested with another implementation of the same interface.

modules.title: HTTP, Forms, and Sessions
modules.description: Build server-side request handling, validation, authentication state, and session-safe workflows.

lessons.title: HTTP Requests and Responses
lessons.description: Read request metadata and construct appropriate HTTP responses.

notes.text: Superglobals such as $_GET, $_POST, $_SERVER, and $_COOKIE expose request-related values. They are external input.
Headers must be sent before the response body.

summary: HTTP handling is a boundary: validate inputs and return deliberate status codes.

lessons.title: Forms and Input Validation
lessons.description: Validate browser-submitted data on the server.

notes.text: filter_input can retrieve and filter external values, but validation rules remain application-specific.
Client-side validation improves usability; server-side validation is the security boundary.

summary: Validation checks whether data satisfies the application's rules; escaping protects a specific output context.

lessons.title: Sessions and Authentication State
lessons.description: Use PHP sessions and understand fixation and cookie-security considerations.

notes.text: PHP's documentation treats HTTP session management as a core web-security concern.
After authentication, session_regenerate_id(true) can prevent reuse of a pre-authentication session identifier.

summary: Session state should contain only what the application needs to recognize the authenticated user.

tasks.title: Secure authentication flow
tasks.description: Implement the server-side authentication portion of a login endpoint.
tasks.problemStatement: Verify a submitted password against a stored hash and regenerate the session ID after success.
tasks.solutionCode:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);
session_start();
$email=trim((string)($_POST['email']??''));
$password=(string)($_POST['password']??'');
$hash=getenv('DEMO_PASSWORD_HASH')?:'';
if(filter_var($email,FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL)&&$hash!==''&&password_verify($password,$hash)){
 session_regenerate_id(true);
 $_SESSION['user_email']=$email;
 echo 'Signed in'; exit;
}
http_response_code(401); echo 'Invalid credentials';
tasks.solutionExplanation: Passwords are verified against a one-way hash and the session identifier changes after successful authentication.

modules.title: Databases with PDO
modules.description: Connect to relational databases, execute parameterized queries, perform CRUD, and use transactions.

lessons.title: PDO Connections and Configuration
lessons.description: Create a PDO connection with externalized credentials.

notes.text: Credentials should not be committed into source code.

summary: Database connection code should be centralized so configuration and error behavior remain consistent.

lessons.title: Prepared Statements and CRUD
lessons.description: Implement database operations using parameters.

notes.text: Prepared statements separate SQL structure from parameter values and are a primary defense against SQL injection when used correctly.

summary: Never concatenate untrusted values into SQL.

lessons.title: Transactions and Data Integrity
lessons.description: Use transactions and database constraints to keep multi-step writes consistent.
learningObjectives: understand foreign keys and unique constraints

notes.text: Transactions group database operations into a unit that can commit or roll back according to the database engine's transaction semantics.
Constraints provide durable data integrity; application checks alone can race with concurrent operations.

summary: Use transactions when a business operation requires multiple related writes to succeed together.

tasks.title: Transactional order workflow
tasks.description: Create an order and its items atomically.
tasks.problemStatement: Insert an order, insert all items, and roll back if any required write fails.
tasks.hint: Keep every related write inside the transaction.
tasks.solutionCode:
<?php
try{
 $pdo->beginTransaction();
 $s=$pdo->prepare('INSERT INTO orders(customer_id) VALUES(:customer_id)');
 $s->execute(['customer_id'=>$customerId]);
 $orderId=(int)$pdo->lastInsertId();
 $i=$pdo->prepare('INSERT INTO order_items(order_id,product_id,quantity) VALUES(:order_id,:product_id,:quantity)');
 foreach($items as $row){$i->execute(['order_id'=>$orderId,'product_id'=>$row['product_id'],'quantity'=>$row['quantity']]);}
 $pdo->commit();
}catch(Throwable $e){
 if($pdo->inTransaction())$pdo->rollBack();
 throw $e;
}
tasks.solutionExplanation: The transaction prevents a partially created order when an item insert fails.

modules.title: Security and Secure Coding
modules.description: Apply PHP security practices to credentials, output, SQL, CSRF, uploads, secrets, and errors.

lessons.title: Password Hashing
lessons.description: Store and verify passwords using PHP's password API.
learningObjectives: allow enough database storage for future hash lengths

notes.text: password_hash creates a strong one-way password hash. PASSWORD_DEFAULT is designed to change over time as stronger algorithms become appropriate; the PHP manual recommends allowing a database field large enough for future values, such as VARCHAR(255).

$hash=password_hash($password,PASSWORD_DEFAULT);
if(password_verify($password,$hash)){ /* authenticated */ }

summary: Never store plaintext passwords or reversible password encryption for normal password storage.

lessons.title: Output Encoding, SQL Injection, and CSRF
lessons.description: Separate validation from output encoding and protect state-changing browser requests.
learningObjectives: encode HTML output in the correct context

notes.text: htmlspecialchars is an HTML output-encoding function; it is not a universal sanitizer for every output context.
SQL parameters protect values, but structural choices such as a sort column still need allow-list validation.
CSRF defenses are needed where a browser can be induced to make an authenticated state-changing request. A server-verified CSRF token is a common defense.

summary: Security controls must match the context: SQL parameterization, output encoding, CSRF tokens, validation, and authorization solve different problems.

lessons.title: Safe File Uploads
lessons.description: Handle uploaded files without trusting filenames or client metadata.

notes.text: Uploaded filenames are attacker-controlled metadata. Generate storage names server-side and treat the original name as untrusted data.
Extension checks alone are insufficient for high-risk uploads; validation should reflect the actual business requirement.

summary: Upload handling is a security boundary and must not become an arbitrary file-write primitive.

lessons.title: Secrets and Error Exposure
lessons.description: Separate deployment configuration from code and prevent sensitive diagnostic leakage.
learningObjectives: avoid exposing paths and SQL details

notes.text: PHP's security documentation emphasizes that both runtime configuration and application code affect security.
Detailed exception traces belong in controlled server-side logs, not user-facing production responses.

summary: Secure deployment includes configuration, permissions, logging, and dependency maintenance.

tasks.title: Harden a login endpoint
tasks.description: Review and implement a secure login flow.
tasks.problemStatement: Use password_verify, session regeneration, validation, and generic failure handling.
tasks.requirements: Do not store or compare plaintext passwords.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The endpoint validates input, verifies a one-way hash, regenerates the session ID, and returns a generic failure.

modules.title: Composer, Architecture, APIs, and Testing
modules.description: Manage dependencies, separate responsibilities, design JSON APIs, and test application logic.

lessons.title: Composer and Autoloading
lessons.description: Use Composer to manage dependencies and load project classes.
learningObjectives: use the lock file for reproducible installs

notes.text: composer.json describes project requirements and autoload rules. composer.lock records a resolved dependency set.
Review dependency changes and test them rather than blindly updating every package in production.

summary: Dependency management is part of application maintenance and supply-chain security.

lessons.title: Dependency Injection and Architecture
lessons.description: Separate HTTP, domain, and persistence concerns and inject dependencies.

notes.text: A small application can separate request handling, application/domain services, and persistence without adopting unnecessary complexity.

summary: Dependency injection reduces hidden coupling and makes replacement in tests straightforward.

lessons.title: JSON APIs
lessons.description: Design predictable JSON endpoints with validation and meaningful status codes.

notes.text: An API contract should define methods, request shape, response shape, status codes, and error semantics.
Do not expose internal exception messages in API responses.

summary: Consistency and safe error boundaries are more important than clever endpoint design.

lessons.title: Testing with PHPUnit
lessons.description: Write focused automated tests and understand unit versus integration tests.
learningObjectives: use test doubles at dependency boundaries

notes.text: Unit tests control dependencies; integration tests answer questions about real database, filesystem, or HTTP integration.

summary: Tests are executable evidence about behavior, not a substitute for design or security review.

tasks.title: Test a repository-backed service
tasks.description: Create a service depending on a repository interface and test it without a database.
tasks.problemStatement: Return a user for a known email and null for an unknown email using a test double.
tasks.requirements: Stub the repository rather than connecting to a real database.
tasks.hint: Keep database access outside the unit under test.
tasks.solutionCode:
<?php
interface UserRepository{public function findByEmail(string $email):?array;}
final class UserService{
 public function __construct(private UserRepository $repo){}
 public function find(string $email):?array{return $this->repo->findByEmail($email);}
}
tasks.solutionExplanation: The service is isolated from database infrastructure and can therefore be tested deterministically.

modules.title: Performance, Deployment, and Final Project
modules.description: Apply measurement-driven performance, supported-version maintenance, and production-oriented deployment practices in a complete project.

lessons.title: Performance and Reliability
lessons.description: Reason about bottlenecks and optimize based on evidence.
learningObjectives: distinguish CPU, I/O, database, and network bottlenecks

notes.text: Performance work should be evidence-driven: measure representative workloads, identify a bottleneck, make a targeted change, then measure again.
Database query shape, indexes, remote calls, filesystem work, and serialization can dominate latency; micro-optimizing PHP syntax is rarely the first step.

summary: Reliable systems optimize the actual bottleneck rather than a guessed one.

lessons.title: Deployment and Version Maintenance
lessons.description: Prepare an application for a production-like environment and plan supported-version upgrades.
learningObjectives: deploy dependencies from a lock file

notes.text: As of September 2026, PHP 8.5 is actively supported. PHP 8.4 is also supported; PHP 8.2 is in security-support-only until 31 December 2026. PHP 8.6 beta is not a production target.
Version upgrades should be tested against the relevant migration guide and application dependencies.

summary: Production maintenance includes supported versions, dependency review, configuration management, backups, logs, and monitoring.

project.name: Secure Task API
project.description: A framework-free PHP task-management API combining typed PHP, validation, sessions, password hashing, PDO, prepared statements, JSON responses, CSRF protection for browser-based state changes, dependency injection, and tests.
steps: Create a Composer project with PSR-4 autoloading.
Create users and tasks tables with unique and foreign-key constraints.
Load database credentials from deployment configuration.
Implement login with password_verify and session_regenerate_id.
Implement authenticated task CRUD with prepared statements.
Issue and verify CSRF tokens for browser-based state-changing requests.
Return consistent JSON and HTTP status codes.
Log detailed exceptions server-side and return generic errors.
Run the application on a supported PHP branch and document deployment configuration.

code.src/Validation.php:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);
namespace App;
final class Validation {
    public static function email(string $email): string {
        $email=trim($email);
        if(!filter_var($email,FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL)) throw new \InvalidArgumentException('Invalid email.');
        return $email;
    }
    public static function title(string $title): string {
        $title=trim($title);
        if($title===''||mb_strlen($title)>200) throw new \InvalidArgumentException('Invalid title.');
        return $title;
    }
}
code.src/Database.php:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);
namespace App;
use PDO;
final class Database {
    public static function connect(): PDO {
        $dsn=getenv('DB_DSN'); $user=getenv('DB_USER'); $password=getenv('DB_PASSWORD');
        if(!$dsn||$user===false||$password===false) throw new \RuntimeException('Database configuration is missing.');
        return new PDO($dsn,$user,$password,[PDO::ATTR_ERRMODE=>PDO::ERRMODE_EXCEPTION,PDO::ATTR_DEFAULT_FETCH_MODE=>PDO::FETCH_ASSOC]);
    }
}
code.public/index.php:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);
require dirname(__DIR__).'/vendor/autoload.php';
use App\Database; use App\Validation;
session_start();
function jsonResponse(array $body,int $status=200): never {
    http_response_code($status);
    header('Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8');
    echo json_encode($body,JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR); exit;
}
try {
    $method=$_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD']??'GET';
    $path=parse_url($_SERVER['REQUEST_URI']??'/',PHP_URL_PATH);
    if($method==='GET'&&$path==='/health') jsonResponse(['status'=>'ok']);
    if($method==='POST'&&$path==='/register'){
        $data=json_decode(file_get_contents('php://input'),true,512,JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
        $email=Validation::email((string)($data['email']??''));
        $password=(string)($data['password']??'');
        if(strlen($password)<12) jsonResponse(['error'=>'Invalid registration data'],422);
        $pdo=Database::connect();
        $s=$pdo->prepare('INSERT INTO users(email,password_hash) VALUES(:email,:hash)');
        $s->execute(['email'=>$email,'hash'=>password_hash($password,PASSWORD_DEFAULT)]);
        jsonResponse(['message'=>'Registered'],201);
    }
    if($method==='POST'&&$path==='/login'){
        $data=json_decode(file_get_contents('php://input'),true,512,JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
        $email=Validation::email((string)($data['email']??''));
        $password=(string)($data['password']??'');
        $pdo=Database::connect();
        $s=$pdo->prepare('SELECT id,email,password_hash FROM users WHERE email=:email');
        $s->execute(['email'=>$email]); $user=$s->fetch();
        if(!$user||!password_verify($password,$user['password_hash'])) jsonResponse(['error'=>'Invalid credentials'],401);
        session_regenerate_id(true); $_SESSION['user_id']=(int)$user['id'];
        jsonResponse(['message'=>'Authenticated']);
    }
    jsonResponse(['error'=>'Not found'],404);
} catch(JsonException|InvalidArgumentException $e) {
    jsonResponse(['error'=>'Invalid request'],400);
} catch(Throwable $e) {
    error_log((string)$e); jsonResponse(['error'=>'Internal server error'],500);
}
code.schema.sql:
CREATE TABLE users (
 id BIGINT UNSIGNED PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
 email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
 password_hash VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
 created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE TABLE tasks (
 id BIGINT UNSIGNED PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
 user_id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
 title VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
 completed BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE,
 created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
 updated_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
 CONSTRAINT fk_tasks_user FOREIGN KEY(user_id) REFERENCES users(id)
);
code.tests/ValidationTest.php:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);
namespace Tests;
use App\Validation; use PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase;
final class ValidationTest extends TestCase {
 public function testValidEmailIsReturned():void {self::assertSame('user@example.test',Validation::email(' user@example.test '));}
 public function testInvalidEmailThrows():void {$this->expectException(\InvalidArgumentException::class);Validation::email('not-an-email');}
 public function testTitleIsTrimmed():void {self::assertSame('Read PHP',Validation::title(' Read PHP '));}
}

project.explanation: The project intentionally exposes core PHP behavior rather than hiding it behind a framework. Registration uses password_hash; login uses password_verify and session_regenerate_id. Database values use PDO parameters. Validation is isolated for unit testing. Detailed exceptions are logged server-side and generic errors are returned. For a browser deployment, add CSRF token issuance and verification to every authenticated state-changing request, enforce HTTPS, configure secure session cookies, protect database credentials, and deploy only supported PHP versions. Task CRUD should use the authenticated user ID in every query so one user cannot address another user's records.
